To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

prenylated G‐proteons (Rac1/Cdc42, Arfs, Rab27A, and Rab27B) regulate insulin granule exocytosis and insulin secretion, and that inhibition of prenylases leads to mislocalization of these G‐protein isoforms to the mitochondria, leading to mitochondrial defects and apoptosis.

prenyl lipidation of GTP‐binding proteins in pancreatic islets plays a critical role in the control of insulin secretion and that this lipidation process is impaired in the β‐cells of diabetic animals and in islets isolated from patients with type‐2 diabetes.

1) small G‐protons are key players in insulin secretion, 2) their post‐transcriptional lipidation is essential for their proper localization and function in GSIS, 3) inhibition of prenyl transferases leads to mislocalization and activation of non‐prenalated small G‐proton in the ER and mitochondria, 4) this leads to ER stress and mitochondrial defects, and 5) these defects lead to loss in GSIS, apoptosis
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the roles of G‐protein signalling networks in the regulation of insulin secretion from islet β‐cells.
the role of G‐protein lipidation in the regulation of islet function, and how defects in these signalling pathways contribute to β‐cell dysfunction and apoptosis in models of diabetes.

understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying the role of G‐protein signalling and its regulation (prenylation and deprenylation) in normal islet function and diabetes, and developing novel therapeutics to halt the progression of diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of G‐protein signalling in β‐cell function is a complex and fascinating story that is just beginning.
the G‐proteome is an important and critical component of the islet signalling machinery and its dysfunction contributes significantly to the pathophysiology of diabetes.
the role of G‐protesins in islet cell function in health and disease is still an area of active research and needs to be further investigated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

G‐proteons are critical for the maintenance of islet function in diabetes and their post‐translationally lipidated forms are critical for their proper localization to appropriate compartments for optimal regulation.
G‐proteons are critical regulators of insulin secretion and their lipidation is a critical post‐translional modification for their optimal function.
prenylation of G‐protesins is a key regulatory event for the normal functioning of β‐cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the G‐protein signalling network in β‐cells is an important regulator of islet function and its defects in the diabetic milieu are likely to contribute to β‐cell dysfunction and apoptosis.
G‐protein prenylation signalling networks are critical for normal islet function, and that defects in these pathways may contribute to the onset and progression of type‐2 diabetes.
G‐protein‐mediated signalling networks in β‐cells are critical for normal islet function in both health and disease, and thus are attractive targets for therapeutic interventions.
